papers.title: Signatures of CH₄ and NH₃ in the atmosphere of β Pictoris b
papers.abstract: β Pictoris is a nearby (19.7 pc), young ( 24 Myr), bright (V = 3.85) planetary system hosting three directly imaged planets. Previous high-resolution spectroscopy of β Pic b has detected H₂O and CO, but not CH₄ or NH₃. Combining observations across a broad wavelength range has been shown to maximise sensitivity to such weak molecular signals. We searched for previously undetected molecular species in the atmosphere of β Pic b using high-resolution near-infrared spectra. We combined 44 CRIRES+ spectral settings covering the H, K, L, and M bands and cross-correlated the extracted planetary spectra with molecular templates. For species with uncertain detectability, we weighted the observations by their molecular information content and data quality, independent of the measured candidate-species cross-correlation functions. We recover H₂O and CO at cross-correlation S/N values of approximately 200 and 50, respectively. We additionally identify tentative CH₄ and NH₃ signals near the expected radial velocity of β Pic b, with S/N values of approximately 5.3 and 5.7. Equivalent extractions at the same projected separation on the opposite side of the star show no comparable peaks. We classify the CH₄ and NH₃ signals as tentative because their cross-correlation S/N values do not fully account for possible residual systematics. If confirmed, these would be the first detections of both species in the atmosphere of β Pic b.

papers.title: JWST Rocky Worlds DDT Observations of LTT 1445 A b and c in Secondary Eclipse Using MIRI/F1500W
papers.abstract: The JWST Rocky Worlds Director's Discretionary Time (RWDDT) program uses secondary eclipse observations to determine the conditions under which rocky exoplanets around M dwarfs retain their atmospheres. We present RWDDT MIRI/F1500W observations of LTT 1445 A b and c, the transiting rocky siblings in the nearest such system (6.9 pc), comprising two eclipses of each planet across three visits. We perform three independent reductions and a joint fit that includes all existing JWST data and 220 radial velocities, improving the precision on the planetary radii, masses, and orbital parameters by factors of 1.6-2.3. We measure eclipse depths of 157⁺¹⁸₋₁₇ ppm and 154⁺⁵⁴₋₃₇ ppm for planets b and c, corresponding to 15 μm brightness temperatures of 528⁺³⁹₋₂₉ K and 625⁺¹⁰⁹₋₇₉ K, both consistent with the dark, bare rock limit. For planet b, combining these data with the archival MIRI/LRS spectrum in a Bayesian retrieval limits the CO₂ partial pressure to <0.6 mbar and the surface pressure to 0.1 bar, while forward models exclude thick aerosol layers that could mimic a bare surface in transmission. We conclude that planet b has no substantial atmosphere. For planet c, a potentially grazing eclipse and overlapping events leave the depth poorly constrained; the data rule out only thick, CO₂-bearing atmospheres (1 bar with ≥1\% CO₂). LTT 1445 A b is the planet closest to the canonical XUV-driven Cosmic Shoreline observed in eclipse so far. Its lack of a substantial atmosphere implies that the Cosmic Shoreline cannot lie much farther toward the airless side than nominally predicted.

papers.title: Hydrolyzed Hazes on Water-rich Exoplanets: Composition and Prebiotic Chemistry
papers.abstract: Although photochemical hazes complicate the spectroscopic analysis of sub-Neptunes, the very presence of hazes can teach us about the habitability of these planets. Aside from affecting a planet's atmospheric and surface dynamics, hazes offer a source of organics potentially including prebiotic molecules like amino acids, nucleobases, and sugars. These organics are particularly compelling for temperate, water-rich planets where hazes may react with liquid water in condensate clouds or surface reservoirs. Hydrolysis reactions drive molecular reorganization and oxygenation, increasing the chemical complexity of the prebiotic inventory. This water-based evolution of hazes in their environment is largely unexplored and will have consequences for their chemical and optical behavior. In this work, we examine the chemical evolution of temperate water-rich exoplanet haze analogs in liquid water. High-resolution mass spectrometry finds thousands of CHNO molecules with bonding behaviors and chemical complexities distinct from the unaltered haze analogs. The oxygen weight percent increases significantly in the soluble fraction and moderately in the insoluble fraction after hydrolysis, with different carbon bonding structures demonstrating the redistribution of functional groups. The hydrolyzed samples exhibit a broader distribution in H/C and O/C ratios, and the molecular formulas suggest complex carbohydrate chemistry that challenges current theories of prebiotic organic delivery.

papers.title: Desorption of water from cosmic silicates
papers.abstract: Recent JWST and ALMA observations of protoplanetary disks have identified water reservoirs in the inner regions of the disks. This would provide terrestrial planets forming therein access to a water reservoir. In situ formation of water molecules on grain surfaces was proposed as one possible formation process in the PDS 70 system, but transport by small silicate particles coupled to the gas could be another mechanism. Laboratory experiments on the thermally induced desorption of water molecules from different water-containing silicates at elevated temperatures provide another possibility for the enrichment of water molecules in the inner disk. Physically and chemically bound water in silicates can be released upon annealing processes. Water that is physically bound undergoes desorption at temperatures up to 473 K. In contrast, chemically bound water in form of different silanol or Mg-OH groups in amorphous silicates or phyllosilicates, can be released at higher temperatures, ranging from 773 to 923 K. The relevant temperatures are sufficient to trigger the solid-state recrystallization of amorphous silicates to Mg-rich orthopyroxene and olivine. The existence of these crystalline silicates has been substantiated through Spitzer and JWST-MIRI observations. Based on the experimental results, we postulate that the desorption of bound hydroxyl groups may serve as a mechanism for the formation of the water reservoir at temperatures up to 900 K, much higher than the water sublimation temperature of 100 to 200 K.

papers.title: A Joint Study of Epoch Astrometry and Radial Velocities of Gaia-4b
papers.abstract: Gaia-4b is the first confirmed exoplanet discovered with Gaia astrometry, based on its identification as a possible exoplanet in the solution in Gaia Data Release 3 and subsequent confirmation with radial velocity. In this work we present a python framework called pyGaiafits that can jointly analyze astrometric time series and radial velocities. We use this to combine the precise along-scan astrometric time series for Gaia-4 from the Gaia DR4 pre-release with 44 radial velocities (RVs) obtained over three years from four independent spectrographs (HPF, HARPS-N, NEID, and FIES). By jointly fitting these two complementary datasets that collectively span a 12-year baseline ( 7 orbital periods of Gaia-4b), we refine the system parameters and determine the true mass of Gaia-4b to be 10.70±0.32 M_J. Critically, we do not find significant evidence for the long-term quadratic RV trend previously reported in the literature, recovering γ = 5.5⁺⁸.³₋₆.₇\;m\,s⁻¹\,yr⁻² consistent with zero. We discuss how this discrepancy likely arises from a degeneracy between orbital period and long-term trends when RVs span only 1.5 orbital cycles --- a degeneracy that is broken by anchoring the ephemeris with early Gaia astrometry.

papers.title: Observational constraints on CO sequestration and disk mass in the planet-hosting PDS 70 disk
papers.abstract: Exoplanets accrete gas, dust, and ice from their natal environment, setting the chemical composition of their atmospheres and interiors. The abundance of the major volatiles in disks can be used to possibly link exoplanet atmospheres to their formation location in the disk. In this work, we aim to quantify the peak CO abundance and disk mass of the PDS 70 disk, the first disk with a direct confirmation of two accreting planets in its dust cavity. We present the first detection of N₂H^+ and C¹⁷O in this disk. The C¹⁷O emission shows marginal statistical evidence for an azimuthal asymmetry trailing that previously seen in the continuum emission. We then compare the disk integrated fluxes of N₂H^+, CO isotopologues, and the continuum to an existing grid of thermochemical models. We find that the derived disk mass drops by a factor of 3.4 from 0.039⁺⁰.⁰⁶⁷₋₀.₀₁₈ M☉ to 0.011⁺⁰.⁰¹¹₋₀.₀₀₆ M☉ if the C¹⁷O line flux is included in the fitting procedure; the quoted intervals do not include systematic uncertainties. CO on the other hand is sequestered with an effective abundance of (4.8⁺⁴.³₋₂.₇ - 17⁺⁸₋₈) × 10⁻⁶ relative to H₂ in the probed disk layers after accounting for CO freeze-out and isotope selective CO photodissociation for the adopted chemical network and ionization prescription. The range in peak CO abundances reflects the uncertainty in the N₂H^+ emission, assuming either optically thin emission at 21 K or optically thick emission. Therefore, the PDS 70 planets are possibly accreting the final portion of their atmospheres from the outer disk molecular layer where CO is sequestered. Thus, CO sequestering may need to be considered when interpreting the chemical composition of planetary atmospheres.

papers.title: Earth accreted increasingly oxidized material as it grew constraining Theia to be small and relatively oxidized
papers.abstract: Many different Solar System formation scenarios successfully reproduce the main astrophysical properties of the inner Solar System. Here, we use the chemistry of Earth's mantle to determine whether proposed Solar System formation scenarios can produce Earth and to constrain the characteristics of both the Proto-Earth and the Moon-forming impactor, Theia. To do this, we use a coupled N-body accretion and core-mantle differentiation model (Rubie et al., 2011, 2015b) applied to a range of proposed formation scenarios (Classical, Annulus, and Grand Tack scenarios). This model calculates the mantle chemistry of Earth-like planets in Solar System formation simulations and adjusts the initial redox state of the building blocks in a synthetic protoplanetary disk until the mantle of the simulated Earth closely matches the bulk silicate Earth. We find that a strong oxidizing gradient among the initial solids of the protoplanetary disk is favored to reproduce the chemistry of Earth's mantle, in agreement with Rubie et al. (2015b). The Solar System formation scenarios examined here successfully reproduce the composition of Earth if two related conditions are met: 1) there is a strong positive oxidation gradient with distance in the inner protoplanetary disk and 2) Earth accretes increasingly more oxidized material (on average) as it grows. Furthermore, in simulations that successfully reproduce Earth's composition, Proto-Earth and Theia may possess a wide range of mantle compositions and mass ratios. However, because late accretion is oxidizing across all proposed Solar System formation scenarios, Theia and Proto-Earth cannot both possess mantles that are more oxidized than the present-day Earth's mantle. Similarly, Theia's mantle may be significantly more oxidized than present-day Earth's mantle, but only if it is relatively small compared to the Proto-Earth.

papers.title: Combining TTVs, RVs, and astrometry to characterize distant giant companions of transiting hot Jupiters: Application to WASP-4
papers.abstract: The origins and architectures of hot Jupiter (HJ) systems remain unclear, with potential explanations for the tight orbits being in-situ formation, disk-migration, or high-eccentricity migration. These mechanisms can leave different imprints on the orbital architecture, but tidal interactions act to erase these imprints for HJs, leading to orbital circularization, realignment, and potentially orbital decay. The latter can be mimicked by the introduction of light travel-time effects (LTTE) caused by an outer giant companion, as for WASP-4\,b. We examine the WASP-4 system using newly obtained ESO\,3.6/HARPS radial velocity (RV) observations and archival transit-timing data, leveraging the LTTE. Furthermore, we present a novel approach of analyzing HJ systems in sight of Gaia's Data Release 4. We propose combining RV, transit-timing, and astrometry data, making use of the LTTE as a proxy for the orbital motion of a possible outer companion. We combine and fit all currently available data and simulate Gaia DR4 and DR5 astrometric measurements of WASP-4 and perform an injection and recovery procedure to estimate their impact on the recovered planetary parameters of WASP-4\,c. The procedure employs a combined model that describes RVs, transit timing variations (TTVs) via the LTTE, and astrometry simultaneously. Analyzing the existing data, we improve the planetary parameters of WASP-4\,c, finding a minimum mass of 9.3±1.7\,M_Jup with an orbital period of 10\,600⁺¹¹⁰⁰₋₁₀₀₀\,d, or about 29\,yr. Furthermore, we find that there is no significant orbital decay taking place for WASP-4\,b. In simulations of Gaia DR5, our three-pronged approach reduces the error bars of WASP-4\,c's parameters by about 10\%, 25\%, and 33\% for its orbital period, time of inferior conjunction, and RV semi-amplitude, respectively. (abridged)

papers.title: OGLE Pre-discovery Observations of the Dwarf Planet Candidate 2026 ED138
papers.abstract: The newly discovered trans-Neptunian object, 2026 ED138, is a strong dwarf planet candidate detected by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Despite its high intrinsic brightness, it evaded detection by previous sky surveys as it hid near crowded Galactic disk fields. Here, we present an analysis of precovery observations of 2026 ED138 in archival data from the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE). We identify 102 reliable detections of the object as it moved across the dense regions of the Galactic plane and bulge between 2011 and 2024. We provide precise astrometric and photometric measurements of the object. Modeling its phase curve yields absolute magnitudes of H_I = 2.224 +/- 0.034 mag and H_V = 3.154 +/- 0.035 mag. Period analysis of the phase-angle-corrected light curve reveals a candidate rotation period of 1.18077 days and its 1-day alias 0.54066 days, although a low signal-to-noise ratio renders these periodicities tentative.

papers.title: Magellan PFS Discovery of a Cold Gas Giant Exoplanet Likely Formed by a Gas Disk Gravitational Instability
papers.abstract: Using the Planet Finder Spectrograph (PFS) on the 6.5-m Magellan Clay Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory we have discovered a cold gas giant exoplanet orbiting the K7V dwarf star HIP88962. 16 yrs of PFS observations imply an exoplanet with an orbital period of ≈ 19.3 yrs and a radial velocity semiamplitude (K) of 94.9 m s⁻¹. With a host star mass of 0.62 M_☉, this implies a planet mass Mₚ sin(i) 5 MJuₚ. While stable M dwarfs have a PFS RMS of ≈ 3 m s⁻¹, the single Keplerian fit for HIP88962 has an RMS of ≈ 6 m s⁻¹, hinting at a second exoplanet. The best double planet Keplerian fit, with a 4.113 d period, still results in a RMS of ≈ 5 m s⁻¹. HIP88962 has Ca II H lines with twice the emission of four stable stars, implying that stellar activity may contribute to the RMS jitter error for the single Keplerian fit. When combined with Hipparcos and Gaia astrometry, HIP88962 b has a nearly edge-on orbit with inclination 91 ± 22 deg, true planet mass 4.83 MJuₚ, semimajor axis 6.15 ± 0.5 au, and eccentricity 0.718 ± 0.02. Including a PFS jitter of ≈ 7 m s⁻¹ yields χ² = 0.995 for the combined solution. A massive gas giant orbiting at ≈ 6 au around a 0.62 M_☉ star is incompatible with published core accretion population synthesis models, but consistent with formation by gas disk gravitational instability.

papers.title: Self-Consistent Microscopic Description of the 146Sm Half-Life for Early Solar System Chronology
papers.abstract: The extinct p-process radionuclide ¹⁴⁶Sm, decaying to ¹⁴²Nd, is a key short-lived chronometer for the formation and early evolution of terrestrial planets and planetesimals. However, there has been a long-standing discrepancy in both the experimental measurements and the theoretical evaluations of the ¹⁴⁶Sm half-life. To address this, a self-consistent microscopic framework for α decay is developed in this work, in which the α particle is treated as a four-nucleon quartet. Its formation amplitude in the nuclear interior is constructed from a coherent superposition of multiple pure single-particle configurations weighted by the pairing occupation amplitudes. Coupling this shell amplitude to the α cluster that survives in the low-density surface region yields a self-consistently determined two-state (shell ⊕ cluster) preformation weight and effective potential. The calculated half-lives for the neighboring emitters of ¹⁴⁶Sm are in good agreement with the measured values. Cross-validation over the neighboring emitters reproduces each excluded half-life without any nucleus-specific adjustment, and yields ¹⁴⁶Sm predictions consistent to within ± 6\% of the resulting half-life T₁/₂=75.1⁺⁶.¹₋₅.₆ Ma. This provides a solid calibration for theoretical studies of the early solar system.

papers.title: Stellar-Field-Driven Induction Heating Unlikely To Cause Significant Heating in Giant Exoplanets
papers.abstract: A planet moving through a changing magnetic field will have a current induced on it by that magnetic field. If the magnetic Reynolds number in the upper atmosphere of this planet is small, the dissipation of this current could result in observable changes to the planet's properties. In this paper, we estimated the total power that would be dissipated in the observed giant exoplanet population if they orbited stars with misaligned magnetic dipoles. We found that, even if all planets orbit stars with extremely misaligned surface magnetic fields, the vast majority of known exoplanets are unlikely to dissipate enough magnetic power to cause observable changes in their surface temperatures. We also extended our calculations to estimate the impact that a low-but-nonzero planetary eccentricity would have on the induced power, and provide a code that implements these calculations. Overall, while it is unlikely that any currently known exoplanets are experiencing a high enough degree of stellar-induced Ohmic heating to be observable, we cannot rule out the possibility that an eccentric, inclined planet on a short-period orbit around a superlatively magnetically active star could have observable magnetic heating. We note that our calculations assume that magnetic diffusion dominates over induction in the upper atmospheres of these planets. However, hot Jupiters with large wind speeds may have high magnetic Reynolds numbers and therefore be in the inductive regime.

papers.title: Dynamical stability of double planets in compact multiplanetary systems
papers.abstract: The "peas-in-a-pod" architecture of planetary systems, where planets are roughly evenly sized and log-spaced, is pervasive throughout known exoplanetary systems. However, many systems deviate slightly from this trend in that they have a "gap" where no planet has been detected, where one might have otherwise expected one to exist. There are many common explanations for the existence of these gaps, including the existence of as-yet-undiscovered planets lurking in these gaps; however, we propose that one potential explanation for some of these gaps is that they are filled by binary planets, a pair of gravitationally bound planets orbiting a common center of mass outside of both bodies. Specifically, in this work, we investigate the dynamical stability of these binary planets as compared to the more conventionally assumed single planets using Monte Carlo N-body simulations. We find that binary planets are slightly less stable than single planets. Overall, we find that binary planets and their cousins in exomoons provide a plausible explanation, at least from a stability perspective, for the existence of some dynamical gaps.

papers.title: Swept by the Galactic Tide: How Galactic Tides and Stellar Encounters Drive the Evolution of Wide Binaries and Their Giant Planets
papers.abstract: Wide stellar binaries (ab > 10³ AU) are common throughout the Galaxy, and many host extrasolar planets. Comparing planets in wide binaries with those around single stars can reveal whether a distant stellar companion affects planet formation. Such a comparison cannot be made directly, however: unlike in single-star systems, the Galactic tide and passing field stars dramatically reshape wide binaries over Gyr timescales, influencing the orbital properties and stability of the planets they host. In this work, we present N-body simulations demonstrating how the Galactic tide and stellar encounters sculpt the orbits of super-Jupiters on 1-6.5 AU orbits in wide binary systems on Sun-like Galactic orbits over 9 Gyr. We predict systematically higher orbital eccentricities for planets in wide binaries compared to single-star systems, with the most significant differences in older systems and those with more massive binary companions. Planetary ejections and disruptions are also common, and we find that planet-hosting binaries with orbits nearly perpendicular to the Galactic midplane are preferentially depleted. In our most optimistic estimate, the maximum hot Jupiter production rate is enhanced by up to a factor of 3 relative to binaries without Galactic perturbations. A significant fraction of these binaries are also ionized (the stars become unbound), with a preference for ionization in lower-mass binaries, while the eccentricity distribution of survivors relaxes from mildly superthermal to nearly thermal. These results provide testable predictions for the population of giant planets in wide binaries soon to be revealed by Gaia DR4 and DR5.

papers.title: Minimum observations for accurate Exoplanetary mass estimation with Radial Velocity Analysis (MINERVA)
papers.abstract: Precise planetary mass measurements are essential for constraining the internal structure and envelope properties of exoplanets and to break key degeneracies in atmospheric retrievals. Estimating the observational effort needed to reach a desired mass precision is therefore fundamental for the optimisation of current and future radial velocity (RV) surveys. We present MINERVA, a tool designed to estimate the required number of RV observations to measure transiting planet masses to a given precision, providing a robust scheduling framework for large-scale samples. MINERVA simulates realistic RV time series for targets orbiting FGKM-type stars. The code ingests real-world observational timestamps to account for weather interruptions and seasonal visibility gaps. To model stellar activity, the pipeline draws ages from local neighbourhood distributions, uses empirical calibrations to derive rotation and magnetic activity levels, and translates these into time-varying RV signals. We also derived a new empirical calibration between chromospheric activity and RV dispersion for K-type stars, using Global Architecture of Planetary Systems (GAPS) and Ariel Mass Survey (ArMS) data. We validated MINERVA on targets with known planetary masses, yielding required observational efforts highly consistent literature values. To demonstrate its capabilities on statistically significant samples, we applied the code to a subsample of the Ariel Mission Candidate Sample. Adopting HARPS-N/TNG as the reference instrument, we estimated the observing nights necessary to achieve a 30% planetary mass precision, providing an optimised observational roadmap for atmospheric characterisation. MINERVA's probabilistic and flexible architecture allows the optimisation of ongoing RV campaigns, the evaluating of undersampling risks in active stars, and the dynamic guidance of population-wide characterisation strategies.

papers.title: Elemental Abundance Trends with Condensation Temperature are Unrelated to Planet Formation
papers.abstract: It has been suggested that the photosphere of the Sun is depleted in the abundances of the refractory elements relative to the photospheres of nearby solar twin stars and that the degree of depletion depends on condensation temperature Tₑₓtc. While the formation of the solar system's terrestrial and/or giant planets may play some role in the refractory depletion of the solar photosphere, it has also been shown that other processes can produce similar results. If the terrestrial and/or giant planet formation explanations are correct, then the depletion of refractory elemental abundances in the photospheres of terrestrial/giant exoplanet host stars should be more pronounced and therefore observable even without achieving the highest possible elemental abundance inference precisions in systems with host star surface convective zones less massive than the Sun's. For stars that host Kepler-discovered systems of terrestrial exoplanets and have low-mass surface convective zones, we do not observe the dependence of depletion on Tₑₓtc predicted by the terrestrial planet formation scenario. For a sample of stars that has been uniformly searched with the Doppler technique for giant exoplanets, we likewise show that giant exoplanet host stars are not depleted but enhanced by about 0.0063± 0.0004 dex in refractory abundances compared to stars of similar masses and metallicities without giant exoplanets. Since gaps opened in protoplanetary disks by giant planets are thought to produce photospheric refractory depletion in their host stars, our observations imply that at constant metallicity giant planets are more likely to form in disks with high refractory abundances.

papers.title: Crater Scaling Relationships for Gas Impingement on Planetary Regolith
papers.abstract: Plume-surface interaction (PSI) effects remains a major uncertainty for operations on regolith-covered planetary bodies. Although spacecraft exhaust can erode surfaces, form craters, and accelerate ejecta, existing PSI relationships are largely derived for scenario-specific lunar and Martian landing conditions and are not yet reliably generalizable. Resolving this problem is important not only for spacecraft safety, but also because controlled thruster interactions could provide an active geotechnical experiment during asteroid reconnaissance. Measurements of thruster-formed craters and ejecta may constrain regolith density, strength, porosity, and particle properties that are otherwise difficult to determine remotely. Such information is particularly relevant to planetary defense, where uncertainty in near-surface properties can strongly affect the outcome of kinetic-impact mitigation and the interpretation of momentum transfer. We investigate gas-driven excavation using near-vacuum, pulsed-N₂ experiments in a cohesionless asteroid regolith analog and comparisons with a low-gravity drop-tower experiment and historical chemical-thruster tests. We adapt projectile-cratering π-scaling, and find that these relationships can describe gas crater volume as a function of gas, target, gravity, and nozzle properties. A common gravity-regime relationship describes the laboratory data and is consistent with an experimental low-gravity result. Generalizing the π-scaling relationship for cohesive targets shows consistency with Apollo-era chemical-thruster cases. These results provide a framework for using spacecraft thrusters as active geotechnical tools during small-body reconnaissance.
